title: The Suffering Servant: Wounded for Our Transgressions
summary: A group of speakers confesses that they despised the Servant, a man of sorrows with nothing attractive about him, and assumed God was punishing him, when in fact he was carrying their sicknesses and was crushed for their iniquities. Silent like a lamb, he is condemned, killed, and buried with the wicked, though he had done no violence. Yet it was the LORD's will: his life becomes a guilt offering, and after his anguish he sees light, justifies many, and is given a portion with the great because he bore the sin of many and interceded for transgressors.
story: This is the heart of the fourth Servant Song, which began at 52:13. In the earlier songs the Servant was chosen to bring justice to the nations (42:1-9), called to restore Israel and be a light to the Gentiles (49:1-6), and beaten for his faithfulness (50:4-9). Now his suffering is explained: it is not punishment for his own sin but the means by which others are healed and forgiven. Chapters 40 to 52 promised that Israel's sin would be dealt with and that the exiles would come home; chapter 53 shows how the deeper problem, sin itself, is dealt with. What follows in chapters 54 and 55 is the result: a restored people, an everlasting covenant, and an open invitation to everyone who is thirsty.
historical:
The song names no historical person, and that silence has driven two thousand years of interpretation. The oldest complete copy of Isaiah, the Great Isaiah Scroll found at Qumran near the Dead Sea in 1947 and copied around the second century BC, contains the chapter essentially as we have it, with a few variants (including “light” in verse 11, which the BSB follows). The Septuagint, the Greek translation made by Jews in the last centuries BC, also has that reading.

Jewish interpretation has taken several paths. The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Prophets, identifies the Servant of 52:13 as the Messiah, but applies most of the suffering to others. Origen, the third-century Christian scholar, reports that in debate a Jewish teacher told him the prophecy spoke of the whole Jewish people as one person, scattered and struck. That collective reading became standard in medieval Jewish commentary through Rashi (eleventh century) and David Kimhi (around 1200), who read the “we” as the nations of 52:15 confessing that they misjudged suffering Israel. Christians from the beginning read the chapter as a portrait of Jesus. Many modern scholars, Jewish and Christian, have proposed further identifications: the prophet himself, a righteous remnant within Israel, or a known figure such as Jeremiah. The hard question below sets out these views.
cultural:
Two assumptions of the ancient world stand behind verse 4. Serious illness and disfigurement were widely taken as signs of divine punishment; Job's friends argue exactly this, and in the law a person with a skin disease had to live outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45-46). So when the speakers saw the Servant diseased and struck down, they concluded he was “stricken by God.” The shock of the song is that they were right that God was involved and wrong about why.

The language of sacrifice would have been familiar to every Israelite. The guilt offering of verse 10 (Hebrew asham) was the sacrifice brought to make restitution for a wrong done, especially against what belonged to God (Leviticus 5:14-6:7). The lamb led to slaughter and the sheep before its shearers (verse 7) came from pastoral life, where animals went to death and shearing without protest. Burial mattered deeply: to be denied an honorable grave was a final disgrace, and verse 9 describes a man assigned a grave among criminals, yet with a rich man in his death.
literary: Taken with 52:13-15, the song falls into five stanzas of roughly three verses each: 52:13-15, 53:1-3, 4-6, 7-9, and 10-12. God speaks in the first and last stanzas (“My Servant”), framing the whole. In the middle stanzas an unnamed “we” speaks, first recalling how they despised the Servant, then confessing what they now understand. Verses 4 to 6 are the turning point, built on a sharp contrast between “He” and “we”: he took our infirmities, we considered him stricken; he was pierced for our transgressions, we all like sheep have gone astray. The vocabulary of sin (transgression, iniquity, sin) and of bearing it (lift, carry, bear) runs through every stanza. The song ends where it began, with the Servant exalted, but now the reader knows the cost. Whether the Servant actually dies is debated, since verses 8 and 9 speak of being cut off and buried while verses 10 to 12 promise he will see offspring and prolong his days; most readers take this as death followed by vindication beyond it.

outline.t: Who has believed? The despised man of sorrows
The confession: he carried our sorrows, we went astray
Silent like a lamb, cut off and buried with the wicked
The LORD's will: a guilt offering, light, and a portion with the great

doctrines.note: The chapter describes one suffering in place of many: “the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all” (verse 6), and his soul is made a guilt offering (verse 10). This is the Old Testament's fullest picture of substitution, and the church has read it as the key to the cross.

The Servant is not called king or messiah in the chapter, yet he is exalted, allotted a portion with the great, and brings righteousness to many. The church confesses that Jesus the Messiah fulfills this role, joining the royal hopes of Isaiah with the Servant's suffering.

“By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many” (verse 11). The many are declared righteous not by their own record but because he bears their iniquities, the pattern Paul develops in Romans.
“Yet it was the LORD’s will to crush Him” (verse 10). The Servant's suffering is the work of human injustice and, at the same time, the purpose of God. The chapter holds both without reducing either.

words.note: Choli, sickness or disease. The BSB renders verse 4 “He took on our infirmities,” and verse 3 calls him “acquainted with grief,” where grief translates the same word. The Servant bears not only sin but its effects in human weakness. Matthew 8:17 applies verse 4 to Jesus's healings, showing that the New Testament read the chapter as covering both.

Saval, to carry a heavy load, used of porters and burden bearers. “Carried our sorrows” (verse 4) and “He will bear their iniquities” (verse 11) use it. Paired with nasa, to lift or bear (verses 4 and 12), it gives the song its governing picture: the Servant shoulders what belonged to others.

Asham, guilt or the guilt offering. In Leviticus 5 and 6 the asham was offered when someone had wronged God or a neighbor, along with restitution. Calling the Servant's life an asham (verse 10) means his death does more than express sympathy: it repairs a real debt of wrong before God.

Paga, to meet, strike, or intercede. In verse 6 the LORD caused iniquity to fall on him; in verse 12 the Servant “made intercession for the transgressors.” The same verb describes both the burden laid on him and the prayer he offers for those who laid it there.

christ: No Old Testament passage is used more directly of Jesus's death. In Acts 8:32-35 an Ethiopian official reads verses 7 and 8 and asks whether the prophet speaks of himself or someone else; Philip begins from this Scripture and tells him the good news about Jesus. First Peter 2:22-25 weaves the chapter into its account of Christ's suffering: he committed no sin and no deceit was in his mouth (verse 9), he bore our sins in his body, by his wounds we are healed (verse 5), and we were straying like sheep (verse 6). Jesus himself applies verse 12 to his arrest in Luke 22:37. John 12:38 and Romans 10:16 quote verse 1 of those who did not believe; Matthew 8:17 applies verse 4 to his healings. Echoes run further: the Son of Man gives his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), Christ was delivered over for our trespasses (Romans 4:25), and he was offered once to bear the sins of many (Hebrews 9:28). Christians have noticed that Jesus was buried in the tomb of a rich man, Joseph of Arimathea (Matthew 27:57-60), after dying between criminals.

hard.q: Who is the Servant, and how can one person's suffering take away another's sin?
hard.a:
The Ethiopian's question in Acts 8:34 is still the first question. Isaiah itself calls Israel God's servant (41:8; 44:1; 49:3), which supports the collective reading held by most Jewish interpreters since the Middle Ages: the Servant is Israel, suffering among the nations, and the “we” are the nations who finally recognize that Israel suffered unjustly and for their sake. A related view limits the Servant to the faithful remnant within Israel. Others take him as an individual: the prophet himself, or a figure such as Jeremiah, the innocent sufferer par excellence. Christians read the Servant as the Messiah, Jesus, noting that in 49:5-6 the Servant has a mission to Israel and so cannot simply be Israel, that he suffers without sin (53:9) while Israel suffered for its sins (40:2), and that his death is voluntary and substitutionary. Many Christian scholars also hold that the collective and individual readings belong together: Jesus is the true Israel, doing as one person what the nation was called to do.

The moral question is real: substitution can sound unjust if it means an innocent third party punished in place of the guilty. The chapter's own answer is that the Servant is not a third party seized against his will. He pours out his life (verse 12), and the song says the LORD's own purpose stands behind his suffering. Christian theology adds that the Servant is God's own presence among his people, so that in the cross God bears the cost himself. Readers who differ on the Servant's identity can agree on what the text claims: the healing of many comes through the wounds of one.

questions: The speakers say “we esteemed Him not” and assumed God was punishing him. When have you misjudged someone's suffering, or had your own misjudged?
Verse 6 says “We all like sheep have gone astray.” Why do you think the confession includes everyone rather than singling out the worst offenders?
How does it change your picture of God that the Servant's suffering is described as both human injustice and “the LORD’s will”?
